Stage 4 · Grammar

The past perfect across a whole story

Knowing the form is one thing. Knowing where to stop using it is the skill this lesson wants.

1 · Look at the guest’s story, retold in full.
From the interview, retold

She had read about the course online months earlier, and she had never held a bird of prey before. When she arrived, the castle had stood there since 1228. A trainer met her at the gate, handed her a glove and told her to keep her arm still. The falcons had been trained for years, so nothing went wrong. She said afterwards that she had felt as though she was in a film.

1 · Read the explanation.
Where the past perfect belongs in a long story

In a story of any length, the past perfect is not spread evenly. It clusters in three places: at the beginning, where you set out what was already true; at any point where you step backwards to explain something; and inside reports of what people said or thought.

Everywhere else, the story runs in the past simple. This is the part that goes wrong at B2: learners who have just learned the form use it for every past event, and the reader loses the thread entirely, because nothing seems to happen in order.

Three tests before you use it
  • Would first or earlier help the reader here? If yes, the past perfect is doing a job. If not, use the past simple.
  • Is there already a time word? Then, afterwards, next and and fix the order by themselves. Before and after do too, which is why the past simple is often enough with them.
  • Am I inside a report? After said, told, realised, discovered, an earlier past shifts back one step: she said she had felt…
2 · Study the examples.
JobExample

opening background, negativeShe had never held a bird of prey.
a state reaching the storyThe castle had stood there since 1228.

Two things to watch

1 — Come forward again. Once the background is set, return to the past simple. A whole paragraph of past perfect reads as though the story has not started yet.

2 — One past perfect can cover several earlier events. She had booked the course, paid for it and told nobody. The first had is enough; repeating it in every clause is heavy and unnecessary.

11 · Read this before the extra practice.
Where the past perfect earns its place

Four jobs, and only four. Opening background: what was already true when the story starts — She had read about the course months earlier, She had never held a bird of prey. A step back mid-story: The falcons had been trained for years. An explanation: Her arm ached, because she had been holding it up for an hour. A reported or realised earlier fact: She said she had felt like a film star, She realised she had left the glove in the hall.

Everything else in the story is past simple. Once you have used the past perfect to reach back, come forward again: a paragraph in which every verb is had + participle stops being a story and becomes a list of prior conditions.

Where to stop

If the order is already obvious, the past perfect is unnecessary. She read about it and then booked it needs no had — and then has done the work. The same is true after before and after: After she arrived, the trainer came out.

Where the order is reversed in the telling, it becomes essential: She booked it because she had read about it. Drop the had there and the reader gets the events in the wrong order.

Two structures pull the past perfect towards them and are worth learning as fixed frames: By the time she arrived, the group had left and It was the first time she had held a bird. A state that reaches into the story, however, often takes the past perfect too: The castle had stood there since 1228.

Errors to watch: She had arrived, then she had signed in and she had met the trainer → the story itself takes the past simple · By the time she arrived, the group left → had left · She said she felt like a film star when you mean the feeling came earlier → had felt.

1 · Read the model.
Model · one recommendation

Nobody I told about it thought it sounded like a holiday. Four days in a fishing village in November, learning to build a small wooden boat, sleeping above the workshop: that is not what people mean when they talk about a week away.

I had booked it in a bad month and had almost cancelled twice. I had never made anything larger than a shelf. On the first morning the man who runs it handed me a plane, watched me use it wrongly for a minute and then took it back without a word. By the second afternoon my hands hurt because I had been sanding the same piece of oak since eight.

Two things are worth knowing. It is genuinely cold, and you are roughing it: one bathroom, no heating in the workshop. And you will not finish a boat. What you take home is a set of joints in a bag and the beginning of a skill.

Book it out of season, when the village is not touristy and the workshop is quiet. Do not book it if you want to relax.
